chunks: What are bond wires?. The question: What are bond wires?
Bond wires are the very thin wires inside a chip package. One end is welded to a pad on the silicon die and the other to a metal leg (lead) of the package.
They are cheap and flexible, so most chips use them. But they are not perfect wires. Each one adds a little resistance and a noticeable inductance, and that affects fast signals.
Picture a long, thin fire hose between a hydrant and a fire truck. A narrow hose limits how much water flows.
A long hose full of heavy water also resists sudden changes: it takes time to get the flow going or to stop it. Resistance is the first effect, and inductance is the second.
A bond wire is a tiny version of that hose for electric current.
One wire-bond cycle. The machine repeats this for every pad, typically many wires per second, which is why wire bonding is cheap per I/O but serial.
Die: the piece of silicon that holds the circuit. Bond pad: a small metal patch on the die where a wire is welded. Resistance: how strongly a wire resists the flow of current.
Inductance: how strongly a wire resists changes in current. Ground bounce: the chip's internal ground voltage jumping when current changes fast.
Take a gold bond wire 25 µm thick (thinner than a human hair) and 3 mm long. It has about 0.
15 ohms of resistance and about 3 nanohenries of inductance, a rule of thumb of 1 nanohenries per millimeter.
Now eight outputs switch 100 milliamps each in 1 nanoseconds through one shared ground wire. The current changes at 0. 8 amps per nanosecond.
The voltage across an inductor is its inductance times how fast the current changes: 3 nanohenries times 0. 8 amps/ns = 2. 4 volts. That is a big jump.
Real chips avoid it with several ground pins, shorter wires and slower edges. That is the whole idea.
"Bond wires are the very thin gold, copper or aluminum wires, typically 15 to 50 microns, that connect pads on the die to the package leads.
A machine welds them with ball and wedge bonds.

They're cheap and flexible, but a few millimetres of wire has roughly a nanohenry per millimetre of inductance and a few tenths of an ohm, so they cause ground bounce and limit high-speed and RF performance.
Power pins use several wires in parallel."
